subject: biology
name: Biology
review_note: Draft written for Quark. Grade levels are typical North American placements and vary by curriculum. Needs review by a subject teacher before it is treated as authoritative.

topics.name: Living things and their needs
learning_goals: Tell living from non-living things.
Describe what plants and animals need to survive.
key_concepts: Needs: food, water, air, shelter, light

misconceptions.description: Classifies moving things as alive and still things as not.
misconceptions.example: Says a car is alive because it moves, and a tree is not.

misconceptions.description: Gives a vague need without saying what it is for.
misconceptions.example: 'Plants need stuff.'

example_problems.prompt: Name three things a plant needs to grow.
example_problems.answer: Water, light and air (carbon dioxide); also nutrients from soil

topics.name: Life cycles
learning_goals: Describe and compare the life cycles of plants and animals.
Order the stages of a life cycle.

misconceptions.description: Puts life-cycle stages in the wrong order.
misconceptions.example: Butterfly: egg, pupa, larva, adult

misconceptions.description: Mixes up names of stages.
misconceptions.example: Calls a tadpole a larva of a butterfly.

example_problems.prompt: Put in order: adult, egg, pupa, larva (butterfly).

topics.name: Plant and animal structures
learning_goals: Identify the parts of plants and animals and their functions.
Explain how structures help survival.

misconceptions.description: Labels a structure incorrectly.
misconceptions.example: Labels the stem as the root.

misconceptions.description: Says an animal grew a feature because it wanted or needed it.
misconceptions.example: 'The giraffe stretched its neck so its babies had long necks.'

example_problems.prompt: What is the job of a plant's roots?
example_problems.answer: Take in water and nutrients and anchor the plant

topics.name: Habitats, food chains and food webs
learning_goals: Describe how living things depend on their habitat and on each other.
Build and interpret food chains and food webs.
key_concepts: Arrows show the direction energy flows

misconceptions.description: Draws food-chain arrows from eater to eaten.
misconceptions.example: fox -> rabbit -> grass

misconceptions.description: Thinks removing one species affects only its direct predator.
misconceptions.example: Says removing grass affects only rabbits.

example_problems.prompt: In grass -> grasshopper -> frog -> snake, which is the producer?

topics.name: Classifying living things
learning_goals: Sort organisms using shared characteristics.
Use and build dichotomous keys.

misconceptions.description: Follows a branch of a key without checking the feature.
misconceptions.example: Takes the 'has wings' branch for a beetle larva.

misconceptions.description: Classifies an animal by habitat rather than features.
misconceptions.example: Says a whale is a fish.

example_problems.prompt: Is a bat a bird or a mammal? Give one reason.
example_problems.answer: A mammal: it has fur and feeds its young milk

topics.name: Human body systems
learning_goals: Describe the main organs and functions of the digestive, respiratory, circulatory and other systems.
Explain how body systems work together.

misconceptions.description: Mislabels an organ.
misconceptions.example: Labels the stomach as the liver.

misconceptions.description: Thinks blood goes to the lungs to make oxygen.
misconceptions.example: 'The lungs turn carbon dioxide into oxygen.'

example_problems.prompt: Which two systems work together to deliver oxygen to cells?

topics.name: Microscopes and magnification
learning_goals: Use a light microscope and prepare a slide.
Calculate magnification and actual size.

misconceptions.description: Multiplies when the formula needs a division.
misconceptions.example: Actual size = image size x magnification

misconceptions.description: Mixes mm and micrometres.
misconceptions.example: Image 20 mm at x400 gives actual size 0.05 um

example_problems.prompt: A cell image is 30 mm long at x600. What is the actual length in micrometres?

topics.name: Cells and cell structures
learning_goals: Describe cell theory and the structures of plant, animal and bacterial cells.
Explain the function of key organelles.
key_concepts: Cell wall and chloroplasts in plants

misconceptions.description: Says animal cells have a cell wall or chloroplasts.
misconceptions.example: Labels a cell wall on a cheek cell.

misconceptions.description: Thinks plant cells have no mitochondria because they photosynthesize.
misconceptions.example: 'Plants make energy with chloroplasts so they don't need mitochondria.'

example_problems.prompt: Name two structures found in plant cells but not animal cells.
example_problems.answer: Cell wall and chloroplasts (also a large central vacuole)

topics.name: Energy flow and matter cycling in ecosystems
learning_goals: Explain how energy flows and matter cycles through ecosystems.
Describe the carbon and nitrogen cycles and energy pyramids.
key_concepts: About 10% of energy passes to the next level

misconceptions.description: Says energy is recycled like matter.
misconceptions.example: 'Decomposers return energy to the soil for plants.'

misconceptions.description: Applies the 10% rule incorrectly.
misconceptions.example: Producers 10,000 kJ, primary consumers 100 kJ

example_problems.prompt: Producers store 20,000 kJ. About how much reaches secondary consumers?

topics.name: Photosynthesis and cellular respiration
learning_goals: Write and explain the overall equations for photosynthesis and aerobic respiration.
Describe where each happens and how they are linked.

misconceptions.description: Thinks a plant's mass comes mainly from the soil.
misconceptions.example: 'The tree is heavy because it absorbed soil.'

misconceptions.description: Thinks plants photosynthesize instead of respiring.
misconceptions.example: 'Animals respire; plants photosynthesize.'

example_problems.prompt: What are the reactants of photosynthesis?
example_problems.answer: Carbon dioxide and water (with light energy)

topics.name: Diffusion, osmosis and membrane transport
learning_goals: Explain diffusion, osmosis and active transport.
Predict what happens to cells in different solutions.

misconceptions.description: Says water moves toward the lower solute concentration.
misconceptions.example: A cell in salt water swells.

misconceptions.description: Thinks particles stop moving at equilibrium.
misconceptions.example: 'At equilibrium diffusion stops.'

example_problems.prompt: A red blood cell is put in pure water. What happens and why?
example_problems.answer: It swells and may burst: water moves in by osmosis to the higher solute concentration inside

topics.name: Mitosis and meiosis
learning_goals: Describe the stages and purpose of mitosis and meiosis.
Compare chromosome numbers in the cells produced.

misconceptions.description: Orders the phases of mitosis wrongly.
misconceptions.example: prophase, anaphase, metaphase, telophase

misconceptions.description: Confuses chromosomes, chromatids and genes.
misconceptions.example: 'Each chromatid is a different gene.'

example_problems.prompt: A cell with 46 chromosomes undergoes meiosis. How many chromosomes are in each gamete?

topics.name: Mendelian genetics
learning_goals: Use Punnett squares to predict offspring ratios for monohybrid and dihybrid crosses.
Interpret pedigrees and non-Mendelian patterns (incomplete dominance, codominance, sex linkage).

misconceptions.description: Puts both alleles of one parent on the same side incorrectly.
misconceptions.example: Writes Aa x aa as AA / aa gametes.

misconceptions.description: Thinks dominant traits are always the most common.
misconceptions.example: 'Polydactyly is dominant so most people have it.'

misconceptions.description: Uses different letters for alleles of the same gene.
misconceptions.example: T and s for tall and short

example_problems.prompt: Two Aa parents are crossed. What is the expected phenotype ratio?

topics.name: Natural selection and evolution
learning_goals: Explain natural selection: variation, inheritance, selection and time.
Use evidence such as fossils, anatomy and DNA to support evolution.

misconceptions.description: Says individuals change because they need to.
misconceptions.example: 'Bacteria became resistant because they needed to survive.'

misconceptions.description: Thinks traits gained during life are inherited.
misconceptions.example: 'Bodybuilders have stronger babies.'

example_problems.prompt: Explain how antibiotic resistance spreads in a bacterial population.
example_problems.answer: Some bacteria already carry resistance; the antibiotic kills the others; survivors reproduce, so resistance becomes common

topics.name: DNA and protein synthesis
learning_goals: Describe DNA structure and replication.
Explain transcription and translation.
key_concepts: Base pairing (A-T, C-G; A-U in RNA)

misconceptions.description: Pairs A with T when transcribing to mRNA.
misconceptions.example: DNA TAC -> mRNA ATG

misconceptions.description: Thinks each cell type has different DNA.
misconceptions.example: 'Muscle cells have muscle DNA.'

example_problems.prompt: Transcribe the DNA template strand TACGGA into mRNA.

topics.name: Population dynamics
learning_goals: Describe population growth, carrying capacity and limiting factors.
Interpret population graphs.

misconceptions.description: Misreads a population graph's scale or axis.
misconceptions.example: Reads the peak as the carrying capacity in a logistic curve.

misconceptions.description: Claims one population causes another's change without evidence.
misconceptions.example: Two populations rose together, so one caused the other.

example_problems.prompt: What is the carrying capacity of an environment?
example_problems.answer: The largest population the environment can support over time

topics.name: Enzymes and biochemistry
learning_goals: Describe the main biological molecules.
Explain how enzymes work and what affects their activity.

misconceptions.description: Says enzymes are used up in reactions.
misconceptions.example: 'The enzyme ran out after one reaction.'

misconceptions.description: Says high temperature kills enzymes.
misconceptions.example: 'The enzyme died at 70 degrees C.'

example_problems.prompt: Why does enzyme activity drop sharply above the optimum temperature?
example_problems.answer: The enzyme denatures: its active site changes shape and the substrate no longer fits

topics.name: Homeostasis, nervous and endocrine systems
learning_goals: Explain negative feedback in homeostasis.
Compare nervous and hormonal control.

misconceptions.description: Describes positive feedback for a negative-feedback system.
misconceptions.example: High blood glucose triggers more glucose release.

misconceptions.description: Confuses glucagon and glycogen.
misconceptions.example: 'Glycogen is the hormone that raises blood sugar.'

example_problems.prompt: What happens when blood glucose rises after a meal?
example_problems.answer: The pancreas releases insulin; cells take up glucose and the liver stores it as glycogen
